findings.title: Entire CSI experiment (Sec. 5.2) has no entrypoint and no SNR metric
findings.claim: The README documents CSI via run_csi.sh, main_csi.py, and inference_csi.py, but none of these files exist in the repo; and no script computes the CSI SNR metric of Eq. 17. Only CSI support modules (`scene/csi_dataset.py`, `scene/csi_model.py`, `gaussian_renderer/render_csi.py`) are present, with no driver that trains, evaluates, or measures SNR.
findings.concern: The complex-valued CSI synthesis result headlined in Sec. 5.2 (mean SNR 20.99 dB, Figs. 7-8) cannot be reproduced from the released code because the training/inference entrypoints and the SNR computation are absent.
findings.resolution: Authors: please add `main_csi.py`/`inference_csi.py`/`run_csi.sh` and the SNR (Eq. 17) computation, or state that CSI results were produced off-repo.

findings.title: BLE KNN localization and RFID AoA (AANN) localization absent from repo
findings.quote: Figure 10 shows that GSRF outperforms NeRF2 by 31.40% on average.
findings.claim: No code implements the fingerprint/KNN localization used for Fig. 10 and Table 3 (localization error), nor the AANN Angle-of-Arrival localization of Appendix F.5. A repo-wide search for localization/fingerprint/KNN/AANN/AoA terms returns no matches (the only `knn` hits are the CUDA `simple_knn` distance init and a split-file name).
findings.concern: The BLE localization result (Fig. 10; Table 3 localization row 0.479 m) and the RFID AoA localization application (F.5) are reported but not reproducible from the released code.
findings.resolution: Authors: please add the KNN fingerprinting localization and AANN AoA scripts, or clarify that these applications were run with external code.

findings.title: No subsampling harness for the sparse (220-instance) and density-sweep RFID runs
findings.claim: Training always draws from the full training set returned by `scene.getTrainSpectrums()`. There is no code (config flag, CLI arg, or sampler) that selects 220 training instances / a 0.8 measurements-per-ft3 subset (Fig. 3) or sweeps measurement density from 0.8 to 15.5 (Fig. 6).
findings.concern: The headline RFID metric comparison (Fig. 3, reported as 21.2% PSNR / 56.4% MSE gain over NeRF2) is measured at the sparse 0.8-density setting, but the released code provides no way to build that sparse training set, so those numbers cannot be reproduced from the config.
findings.resolution: Authors: please add the density/instance subsampling used for Figs. 3 and 6 (e.g. a `--num_train`/`--density` option).

findings.title: Runnable RFID/BLE renderer is a softmax blend, not the paper's complex CUDA ray tracer
findings.quote:
mahalanobis = torch.einsum('rni,nij,rnj->rn', offsets, precision, offsets)
        weights = torch.softmax(-0.5 * mahalanobis + log_attenuation.unsqueeze(0), dim=1)
        rendered_chunks.append(weights @ stacked_signal)
findings.claim: `render_rfid` imports `ComplexGaussianTracer` (line 3) but never calls it; instead it aggregates Gaussians with a per-ray softmax over all Gaussians (a normalized weighted average of complex radiance), with attenuation entering as a single real log-weight. This is neither the depth-sorted cumulative-transmittance product of Eq. 14 nor a call to the CUDA tracer. All four runnable entrypoints (`train_rfid.py`, `inference_rfid.py`, `main_ble.py`, `inference_ble.py`) use this function; the CUDA tracer is wired only into `render_csi` (which has no entrypoint — see csi-experiment-not-runnable).
findings.concern: The paper's third contribution — a complex-valued CUDA ray-tracing algorithm — is not exercised by any runnable experiment, so the reported RFID/BLE fidelity and latency numbers (Figs. 3-5, 9, 11-12; the '4.18 ms hybrid CUDA-based ray tracer') are produced by an unmentioned softmax renderer, and the paper's efficiency/interference mechanism does not describe the code that generated them.
findings.resolution: Authors: confirm whether the released RFID/BLE numbers were produced by `render_rfid` (softmax) or by the CUDA tracer; if the latter, release the code path that invokes it for RFID/BLE.
findings.paper_ref: Eq. 14; Contributions list (Complex-Valued Ray Tracing); Fig. 5

findings.title: Transmittance is a single real sigmoid scalar, not the claimed complex ρ ∈ C
findings.claim: Each Gaussian's transmittance/attenuation is a single scalar (`_attenuation` has shape [N,1], activated by `torch.sigmoid` at line 38), so it is a real number in [0,1] with no phase. The paper (Sec. 4.2 and Appendix A) defines transmittance as complex, ρ = |ρ|·e^{j∠ρ} with a phase shift ∠ρ = −β·Δt.
findings.concern: One of the two headline 'complex-valued attributes' (transmittance) is real in the implementation, so the phase-shift-through-medium physics described in Eq. 14 / Appendix A is not modeled; only the radiance carries phase.
findings.resolution: Authors: clarify whether transmittance phase was intended; if so, the parameter must be complex (two channels), which it is not in `gaussian_model.py`.

findings.title: Released configs set FLE degree 9 (100 coeffs); paper states L=3 (16 coeffs)
findings.claim: The released rfid/exp1.yaml (and `ble`/`csi` configs) set `fle_degree: 9`, giving (9+1)^2 = 100 FLE coefficients per channel. The paper states the model uses degree L=3 (16 coefficients) and its own study (Table 4) recommends L=3, calling L>=5 overfitting-prone.
findings.concern: The config that the README says produced the released weights contradicts the paper's stated model capacity and its FLE-degree recommendation, so the released model does not match the described 16-coefficient GSRF.
findings.resolution: Authors: confirm the FLE degree used for the reported numbers; if L=3, correct the released configs (they set 9).
findings.paper_ref: Section 5.4 ('degree of L = 3, resulting in 16'); Appendix F.3 / Table 4

findings.title: Configs use an 80/20 split; paper states 70/30
findings.claim: All three configs set `ratio_train: 0.8` (80% train / 20% test), consumed by `split_dataset_random` and the BLE/CSI loaders. The paper states the RFID and CSI datasets are 'randomly split into 70% for training and 30% for testing'.
findings.concern: The released train/test ratio differs from the ratio described in the paper, changing both the amount of training data and the size of the evaluation set.
findings.resolution: Authors: confirm the split ratio used for the reported numbers (70/30 per the paper, vs 80/20 in the configs).
findings.paper_ref: Section 5.1 and 5.2 ('70% for training and 30% for testing')

findings.title: BLE trains on mean-amplitude with squared error; paper describes a ray-sum with L1
findings.quote:
pred_amp = spectrum.mean()
        gt_amp = viewpoint_cam.spectrum.cuda().mean()

        loss = (pred_amp - gt_amp) ** 2
findings.claim: For BLE (single-antenna RSSI) the predicted signal is the mean over the rendered spherical grid and the loss is squared error on that mean. The paper's SINGLE ANTENNA case defines the synthesized signal as the sum over rays (Ŝ = Σ_u Σ_v Ŝ_{u,v}) and the real-valued loss as L1 (|Ŝ − S|_1).
findings.concern: The single-antenna aggregation (mean vs sum) and loss (L2 vs L1) differ from the paper's stated formulation; both are individually reasonable, but the code does not match the described procedure.
findings.resolution: Authors: reconcile the BLE aggregation/loss with the SINGLE ANTENNA definition in Sec. 4.4 (sum + L1).

findings.title: BLE split makes the test set a subset of the training set (100% leakage)
findings.quote:
num_train = int(num_samples * ratio_train)
        num_test = num_samples - num_train
        train_set = set(all_indices[:num_train].tolist())
        test_set = set(all_indices[:num_test].tolist())
findings.claim: The BLE loader takes `train_set = all_indices[:num_train]` and `test_set = all_indices[:num_test]` from the SAME shuffled array. Since num_test = num_samples − num_train ≤ num_train, the test indices are a prefix of the train indices, so every test transmitter is also in training. My check (`_audit_code/check_ble_split_overlap.py`) reproduces the slicing and finds 1200/1200 = 100% of test samples in train at N=6000, ratio 0.8 (correct `[num_train:]` split gives 0 overlap). The correct line is `all_indices[num_train:]`.
findings.concern: Every BLE RSSI evaluation sample was seen during training, so the reported BLE numbers (Fig. 9 / Table 3: 4.09 dBm error, '32.79% improvement over NeRF2', and the localization result) reflect training-set memorization rather than generalization, invalidating the BLE headline comparison.
findings.resolution: Fix the test slice to `all_indices[num_train:]`, regenerate the split, and re-run BLE training/eval; report whether the RSSI error and NeRF2 gap survive a disjoint split.
